World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Patients in need of home pharmacy help missing out due to caps
World.content:
When Mildura resident Bronwen Walker was offered an in-home review of her medication, she took it up immediately.

"I was taking three [tablets] in the morning and three at night, and that was just one tablet. Then I had all the other tablets I'm taking, and some of those were doubled up each day," she said.

"I'm certainly on a lot of medication, and I'd had a couple of incidents where it was almost the equivalent of an overdose."

Home Medicine Reviews are available across Australia and aim to minimise incorrect medication use by helping people better understand and manage their medicines.

Mildura pharmacist Brooke Shelley is one of a few pharmacists who can provide the service in the Mallee region of north-west Victoria and regularly visits patients, including Ms Walker.

Bronwen Walker is now on less medication thanks to reviews by Brooke Shelley. (Supplied: Brooke Shelley)

Ms Walker said Ms Shelley worked with her GP to reduce the number of medications she was on, and she soon started to notice positive changes to her quality of life.

Ms Shelley is one of many pharmacists calling for funding changes that would allow her to deliver the "life-saving" service to more people.

Pharmacists in 'unfair situations'

Pharmacists are limited to providing 30 government-funded at-home reviews every month.

Once she has reached the 30-patient limit, Ms Shelley must choose between turning people away, charging patients or working without pay.

"These caps really unfairly put professionals in an unfair situation where they're having to choose who receives care," she said.

"Medication problems don't wait until the first of the month. Patients shouldn't have to either.

"We would never accept that a patient with a breast lump is being told by their GP that they have to wait for a mammogram because the number of referrals that month has already been exceeded."

Brooke Shelley is also the national board director of the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia. (Supplied: Brooke Shelley)

Ms Shelley said there were higher rates of chronic disease in the Mallee, most of which required medication.

Ms Walker said she knew many people who would benefit from a medication review, but due to patient limits, they had not been able to access one.

"I've got friends on a lot of medication, and I'd suggested perhaps they could see Brooke, but she couldn't take that up because she'd reached her limit," she said.

Costs increasing

Ms Shelley said funding for at-home medication reviews had not been indexed since 2019, and many pharmacists could not sustain it as a full-time career path despite extra postgraduate training.

She said it had become tough to deliver the service, with increased costs for items such as fuel and the inability to consult via telehealth.

Brooke Shelley says telehealth was funded under the program during the pandemic. (Supplied: Brooke Shelley)

A travel allowance is provided to pharmacists for round trips of 200 kilometres or more, but the flat payment of $125 does not increase regardless of the total distance.

Some of Ms Shelley's patients live more than 100km away, but the service was not funded unless she stepped foot in their home.

"I want to be in the home, that's where we do our best work. But the reality is if we can't be in the home, they will receive no care," she said.

" In rural areas, telehealth is not something we do for convenience. We do it to improve access. "

Ms Shelley said nearly $20 billion was spent in Australia on medicine every year, but less than 1 per cent of that went towards medication safety programs.

"We're not asking to increase that by billions," she said.

"We're really just saying, let us do more, pay us not at 2019 rates, make sure that we can do this work and be recognised for the challenges of driving distance in the country and being able to be as productive as we possibly can."

Patients 'falling through cracks'

Last month, the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia (PSA) urged the federal government to reinstate telehealth funding for home reviews.

The society said pharmacists were concerned about their ability to access and afford fuel.

"The support these patients need, such as medication reviews, is becoming rapidly unsustainable amid the current fuel crisis, unless the government reinstates telehealth," PSA national president Mark Naunton said.

"We know telehealth worked effectively and efficiently during the COVID-19 pandemic, so why not now?"

Mildura has a higher-than-average proportion of residents aged over 65. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A government spokesperson said it had increased the cap from 20 to 30 patients in 2020, and additional reviews could be done at the patients' expense if requested.

"The monthly cap helps ensure the HMR program is sustainable and allows each pharmacist to deliver reviews for the patients who need them most, in their homes," they said.

The spokesperson said they were unable to pre-empt whether any changes would be announced in the upcoming federal budget.

World.title: Alice Springs 5yo's alleged murderer's first court appearance streamed live
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.

The man charged with the murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby will face court for the first time this morning, with the hearing marking the first time a Northern Territory criminal proceeding is live-streamed to the public.

Jefferson Lewis, 47, was arrested on Saturday after the five-year-old girl went missing from an Alice Springs town camp last month, sparking a five-day search.

Today's proceedings will be streamed live online, in a first for criminal courts in the NT. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Mr Lewis is facing one count of murder and two other charges that cannot be published for legal reasons, and will appear in the Alice Springs Local Court via audio-visual link after 9:30am.

The NT Courts social media account has published a link to the live-stream online due to the high level of interest in the case, which can be accessed here.

Dozens of Alice Springs residents joined police and emergency services in the search for the little girl before her body was found on April 30, about 5 kilometres south of where she was last seen.

In announcing the charges on Sunday, NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole said detectives had been working "around the clock" since Mr Lewis's arrest.

The five-year-old's family has requested that she be referred to as Kumanjayi Little Baby since her death. (Supplied: NT Police)

"This remains a deeply distressing matter, and our thoughts are firmly with Kumanjayi's family, loved ones and the wider community that have been deeply impacted by these events," he said.

Kumanjayi's kinship grandfather told the ABC his family was in "sorry business" and urged the community to "let the justice system do its work".

World.title: Calls for NSW government-run DV body to solely provide services
World.content:
A new campaign is calling for a NSW government-run domestic violence (DV) body to solely provide services rather than independent organisations, though the idea has raised concerns from the peak body.

The Public Service Association of NSW (PSA) said the state needed to build a public sector for DV services delivered as a core government function alongside policing, housing, health and child protection.

The union's general secretary, Stewart Little, said support for victim-survivors had been outsourced to non-government organisations (NGOs).

He described it as a fragmented model.

"We're in the middle of a domestic violence crisis," he said, also pointing to the rise in incarceration rates related to changed bail laws.

"You've got some fantastic NGOs that are out there doing their best … but they don't have certainty when it comes to long-term funding, relying on grants.

"We need a public sector response to this crisis."

Mr Little says accountability is being outsourced when NGOs, and not a government body, run the state's domestic violence services. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

The majority of DV services across the states and territories are managed by community-run, faith-based or non-faith-based NGOs, which are often then funded in part by the state and federal government.

"When safety is outsourced, accountability is outsourced," Mr Little said.

" Some women get comprehensive support. Others get a phone number and a waiting list. "

For the many NGO-run DV services who receive some amount of government funding, they are required to comply to government accountability frameworks, such as detailing how funds are spent.

Governments do not have a role, however, in how the NGO-run service is governed or how daily service is delivered.

Many NGO-run DV services are required to comply to accountability frameworks, particularly when it comes to financial transparency. (Supplied)

The 'gold standard' example

The Western Sydney Nepean Blue Mountains Domestic Violence Service (WSNBMDVS) supports the Blacktown, Penrith and Mount Druitt area, which has high rates of DV-related assault.

The PSA, which represents many WSNBMDVS workers, said the service gets its staff from a pool of child protection caseworkers and the Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ).

It is the only DCJ-run DV service in NSW.

"It was specifically designed to set a gold standard in domestic violence service," Mr Little said.

The WSNBMDVS service provides ongoing support to victim-survivors in the wider Mount Druitt area. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Stephanie, whose name has been changed for privacy reasons, previously worked at the WSNBMDVS for a number of years and was a member of the PSA.

"It's a one-stop shop for people fleeing domestic violence," she said of the service.

"The work is so rewarding."

She agreed a government DV services body should operate, but in conjunction with the assistance of NGOs.

"I think it's a good thing for government to fund it, because then they're going to be able to be held accountable. However, there is definitely room and a need for both NGOs and a [government-run service]," Stephanie said.

Peak body credits current services

Domestic Violence NSW (DVNSW) is the peak body for DV services in NSW.

Angie Gehle says refuges across the state have localised knowledge and operate with high standards and a DV-informed approach. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Their senior policy and advocacy officer, Angie Gehle, said DVNSW viewed the PSA's campaign as a "huge shift backwards".

"It implies that specialist domestic and family violence services are operating without standards or accountability, which is just not true," she said.

" It risks undermining 50 years of advocacy by the domestic and family violence sector. "

DVNSW is currently contracted by the NSW government to lead the development of the Specialist Domestic and Family Violence Quality Standards for the sector.

Ms Gehle feared Indigenous victim-survivors in NSW would not feel comfortable with a government-run service, with their distrust rooted in a legacy of colonial discrimination.

"With an over-governed sector structure and First Nations women … we are concerned we would see a decline in help seeking and a decline in reporting of domestic violence offences."

Woman hospitalised after DV assault had her baby taken away A new report into the massive over-representation of Indigenous children in out-of-home care in Western Australia reveals how factors like homelessness and DV can lead to mothers having their babies taken away.

Mr Little suggested a workaround would be to mirror a DV public service sector with the current health sector — being run by government, but liaising with local community organisations.

Ms Gehle said NGOs were often best-placed to respond to people facing additional barriers to accessing government systems, and credited their localised knowledge and grassroots work.

"It's quite an elitist and privileged way of looking at the service structure … we know that the NGO sector provides such life-saving support, and they do it in a DV-informed way," Ms Gehle said.

" We are united in a shared mission to end domestic and family violence. If we believed this approach would get us there, we would support it. "

Jodie Harrison says the state government values the contributions of advocates, victim-survivors, the sector and stakeholders. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

In a statement, Minister for the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault Jodie Harrison noted the government was aware of the PSA's campaign.

"We are taking a whole-of-government and whole-of-community approach to address domestic and family violence in our state, and we continue to work with advocates, victim-survivors, the sector and stakeholders in our responses," she said.

"The Government is also in the process of rolling out five-year contracts for key programs so that the sector has funding certainty and to strengthen victim-survivors continuity of care.

" We know there is more to do. "

'It's not a practical suggestion,' says NGO

Yvette Vignando is the CEO of Mary's House Services, a northern Sydney refuge which provides accommodation and services for women and children escaping DV.

The NGO is a registered charity almost entirely philanthropically funded, though they had received some state government funding to add three caseworkers to their team.

"We are underfunded, there are not enough services in certain parts of the state and demand keeps increasing," Ms Vignando noted.

"I understand why the Public Services Association is calling for solutions. But it's not a practical suggestion, given the way the cycle of politics works and given the number of NGOs across Australia who are already providing services, and the community members and funders who are happy to provide support for those services."

Yvette Vignando says Mary's House Services has provided more than 18,000 safe room nights to women and children escaping violence since 2016. (Supplied)

Ms Vignando said the reason Mary's House Services existed in the first place was because local community members were concerned with the lack of services for victim-survivors in the area and had felt the need to step up due to a lack of government action.

She said Mary's House Services, and some other similar NGOs who did not receive significant government funding, did not have their data collected by the state government — such as the number of women and children who visit the refuge.

"The solution has to start with the government having an accurate sense of the level of demand," she said.

With the state budget imminent, Ms Gehle said it was crucial to prioritise the sector's overarching message to increase core funding for its current services.

"It's really about uplifting the incredible work that our specialist services are doing on the ground now," she said.

World.title: 'Chocolate experience' to be housed in building inspired by foil wrappers
World.content:
A "chocolate experience" to be housed in a building inspired by foil chocolate wrappers has been approved by Glenorchy City Council's planning authority.

The $150 million proposal, which includes a chocolate lab, chocolate lounge, emporium and tasting opportunities, would be built at the Cadbury factory site in Claremont, Hobart's northern suburbs.

"The chocolate experience will undoubtedly be a major tourism drawcard, generating economic activity during both construction and through increased visitor numbers in the longer term," Glenorchy Mayor Sue Hickey said.

" The old chocolate factory shut down a decade ago, but even now, people still remember so fondly going and visiting. "

An artist's impression of the central atrium of the proposed chocolate experience. (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

Factory tours, which had been a popular visitor drawcard, were stopped at Cadbury in 2008 following changes to health and safety laws.

Cadbury's parent company, Mondelez International, closed the factory's visitor centre in 2015.

Councillor Hickey said she was looking forward to visiting the new attraction.

"Everybody will be. All the locals will be queuing up … it's going to be of international significance," she said.

Many people fondly remember factory tours at Cadbury. (ABC News)

The developers behind the chocolate experience proposal, Simon Currant & Associates, have said their proposal "will bring back to life one of Tasmania's most beloved attractions: the Cadbury factory site at Claremont".

A spokesperson for the developers said the chocolate experience would attract more than 430,000 visitors a year.

The developers behind the chocolate experience say it "will bring back to life one of Tasmania's most beloved attractions". (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

'A reinvention of the chocolate factory'

The inspiration for the building's exterior came from foil chocolate wrappers.

"Just as peeling back foil reveals a rich, indulgent centre, the interior of the Chocolate Experience offers a striking contrast to its outer shell," project architects Cumulus Studio wrote in a report to the Glenorchy City Council.

"Stepping inside, guests move from the building's nondescript, reflective exterior into a hidden, sensory-rich world."

The facade of the proposed building takes its inspiration from foil chocolate wrappers. (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

The Cumulus report says that the "visitor experience is envisaged as a three-hour ticketed visitor journey … blending storytelling, technology, and hands-on participation to create an active, sensorial journey for all ages".

"The journey begins in Chocolate Central, where a responsive LED whirlpool of virtual chocolate draws guests into the experience.

"Augmented reality photo moments and multi-sensory 'pipe satellites' immerse visitors in sight, sound, aroma, taste, and touch before they continue deeper into the story of chocolate."

An artist's impression of the central atrium of the proposed chocolate experience. (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

Next, there would be a series of "immersive zones".

"The Tropical House evokes a twilight cacao forest with interactive viewfinders and projection columns that bring pollinators and wildlife to life, while the Laboratory invites hands-on exploration of chocolate-making through films, machines, and tactile exhibits, culminating in the vibrant Paint Your Flavour room.

Concept art for interior of the proposed Cacao Forest. (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

"The playful Factory Control Room gamifies production, the Taste Kitchen serves as an 'island of taste and sensation,' and the Premium Chocolate Studio offers a close view of artisan chocolatiers at work."

Visitors would be able to extend their journey with "premium activations", including a build your own chocolate bar workshop and 45-minute masterclasses.

Visitors will have the option of a 45-minute chocolate masterclass. (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

There would also be a lounge, a cafe, and an emporium.

"At its essence, the Cadbury Experience is a reinvention of the chocolate factory — a place where industry dissolves into imagination and where the pragmatic meets the poetic," the Cumulus report reads.

An artist's impression of the proposed chocolate lounge. (Supplied: Cumulus Studio)

Originally, the proposal included plans for the world's tallest chocolate fountain, which was first publicly announced during the 2024 Tasmanian election campaign when Premier Jeremy Rockliff promised $12 million in staged public funding for the developer, Simon Currant & Associates.

The fountain, however, did not appear in plans lodged with the Glenorchy City Council in August last year.

The chocolate experience would be built next to the Cadbury factory at Claremont in Hobart's northern suburbs. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

While the fountain and broader chocolate experience proposal was first made public in 2024, documents obtained under Right to Information showed it had been circulating within the State Growth Department for several years.

Documents also showed the developer received two grants in 2022, totalling $150,000 — which were not publicly disclosed and were retrospectively placed under grant schemes — to help fund a demand study, update financial figures, and develop a public relations strategy.

According to the Cumulus report, Mr Currant's company took on the project in 2021 and commissioned a series of tourism demand studies in 2022.

The developers plan to have the chocolate experience open late in 2028.

World.title: Bishop ordered to resign over relationship with priest appealing decision
World.content:
One of South Australia's most senior Anglicans has been stripped of his position over an undisclosed relationship with a priest he ordained, in a case described by the church as "a gross ethical failure".

Following a lengthy investigation, the Anglican Episcopal Standards Board concluded Bishop Keith Dalby breached his ordination vows of honesty, fidelity and integrity.

It found him unfit to hold office and ordered that he either resign or be "deposed from Holy Orders".

But the bishop told the ABC he had lodged an appeal against the decision, which he described as "harsh and disproportionate".

Bishop Dalby was in charge of the Diocese of the Murray, one of three Anglican dioceses in South Australia, when he became "romantically involved" with aspiring priest Alison Dutton in early 2023.

Over the following months, he participated in several decisions related to her career within the church, including supporting her candidacy for priesthood, nominating himself as her direct supervisor and suggesting payments for her.

He ordained her in August 2023 — 10 days before the pair married in a secret civil ceremony in Queensland and then honeymooned in Thailand.

The ordination of priest Alison Dutton (front, left) and three others by Bishop Keith Dalby (second row) in August 2023. (Supplied: Diocese of Adelaide)

Bishop Dalby did not disclose the relationship to the church until December, at which point he was asked by the Diocesan Council to resign.

He refused and was stood down for more than two years while investigations were underway.

Bishop's position 'untenable'

At hearings in March, the Episcopal Standards Commission, an arm of the church, told the board Bishop Dalby had repeatedly breached the code of conduct for Anglican clergy.

"These were not isolated and unintentional lapses," the commission said, according to a published judgement.

"They reveal an intentional pattern of deception and concealment, misuse of his authority, and a gross ethical failure over at least a nine-month period.

"His position is, with respect, untenable."

The commission also alleged the bishop on several occasions threatened to punish those who opposed his views and "vented his anger towards others by belittling them".

The bishop of the Diocese of the Murray is based at St John the Baptist Anglican Cathedral in Murray Bridge. (Supplied: The Murray Anglican)

In his evidence, Bishop Dalby was reluctant to accept characterisations that he had bullied or threatened anyone.

He said his relationship with Reverand Dutton formed over time rather than beginning as a "fixed and fully formed commitment", and he did not fully appreciate its implications.

While he understood he would ultimately need to disclose the relationship, he said he struggled with the timing and manner of that disclosure.

The bishop accepted responsibility for his "culpability and lack of candour", but said his motives were not malicious and the evidence did not show he was unfit for office.

Board orders resignation

In its April judgement, the board concluded Bishop Dalby had irreversibly eroded the trust between the clergy and congregation of the diocese.

It found him unfit to hold any ordained role, and ordered that he resign within 21 days or face deposition.

But the direction will not be enforced while his appeal is underway.

In a statement to the ABC, Bishop Dalby accepted the seriousness of the board's findings but said he felt its conclusion was unduly harsh.

The Right Reverend Mark Short says the church is committed to appropriate professional conduct. (Supplied: Anglican Diocese of Canberra and Goulburn)

"I acknowledge that this constituted a significant error of judgement and a failure to meet the standards expected of me as a bishop of the church," he said.

"While I did not intend harm, I acknowledge that intention does not lessen the consequences of my actions."

The Right Reverend Mark Short, leader of the Anglican Church of Australia, acknowledged the appeal, which he said would be considered by the review tribunal as soon as possible.

"The Anglican Church of Australia is committed to appropriate professional conduct by those entrusted with ordained and lay ministry and to ensuring that any complaint is taken seriously and dealt with properly," he said.

World.title: Who pays to put food on the table during a global crisis?
World.content:
Questions are being raised about who pays to ensure Australians have enough food on the table during a global crisis.

Supermarkets are still expecting big profits while food insecurity rises and many of the country's farmers struggle to break even.

Georgia Schuback, 25, from Port Macquarie shops around between three different supermarkets.

"If I didn't do this, we wouldn't have as much food. We wouldn't have as much money," she said.

Woolworths and Coles are being urged to absorb more of the cost increases from the Iran war. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Growers are also stretched, as high fuel and fertiliser prices squeeze already tight margins.

"Many of them will unfortunately be looking at potentially going into even more debt," New South Wales Farmers Association economist Sam Miller said.

Price increases 'not shared fairly'

Woolworths's Australian food sales reached $13.8 billion in the three months to early April, up 6 per cent compared to the same time last year.

Coles supermarket sales were also up 4 per cent in a similar timeframe, to $9.8 billion.

Mr Miller said he was concerned the price increases were not shared "equitably and fairly" from the farmer to the consumer.

"The input cost pressures on farmers are incredible, and it's just not being reflected in the price that they're getting," Mr Miller said.

" I don't think it's acceptable … that the only people in the supply chain that see their business profits go up are supermarkets. "

The supermarket giants are not strangers to price and profit scrutiny.

In March 2025, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) found the country's supermarkets were some of the most profitable in the world.

Federal court cases against Coles and Woolworths, accused separately by the ACCC of fake discounting, are awaiting judgement.

Coles and Woolworths say they are supporting shoppers. (ABC South East SA: Samuel O'Brien)

Last week, Woolworths put a freeze on the price of 300 products for the next three months, to support shoppers dealing with cost-of-living pressures.

A Coles spokesperson said its approach was to "absorb costs where we can and [to] continue to review prices regularly".

"Our autumn value campaign, launched in March, lowered prices on around 400 lines, including products such as chicken, lamb and coffee," the spokesperson said.

"We are also working closely with Australian farmers and suppliers."

Supermarket power

University of Melbourne food systems expert Rachel Carey said most Australians bought their food at supermarkets.

"A very small number of supermarkets have a very large share of that grocery market," Dr Carey said.

"Fundamentally, we need to be questioning the power of the major supermarkets.

"That really comes back to also diversifying our food supply chain … [and] looking at other approaches that give farmers more control over their supply chains."

Rachel Carey says Australia needs to diversify food supply chains. (Supplied: University of Melbourne)

Food rescue charity OzHarvest has warned that the jump in the number of people going without meals since the Iran conflict began was likely to worsen.

"The signs are deeply concerning," chief executive James Goth said.

"Food is the only flexible variable in a household budget. It's the first thing to go when times get tough, and that's exactly what we're seeing."

Woolworths provides 60 per cent of OzHarvest's rescued food, which Mr Goth welcomed, but he said: "It's not enough to keep pace with the extraordinary surge in need we're seeing."

"Supermarkets are a critical part of the food system and the safety net, and it's important all parts of the system play a role in supporting Australians," he said.

OzHarvest is concerned food insecurity will worsen. (ABC News)

Shoppers 'grin and bear it'

Back at the supermarket in Port Macquarie, Kath Menz and Phillip Hill have noticed the uptick in grocery prices.

"Everything else [is] going up, so what can you do? You just have to grin and bear it," Ms Menz said.

Mr Hill said he would not mind the higher prices if the money went back to farmers.

"Even though the retailers do a good job, the farmers are the backbone of the industry," Ms Menz said.

" [Farmers] have to be looked after because they feed us. "

Phillip Hill wants farmers to be paid fairly. (ABC Rural: Lauren Bohane)

As farmers make hard decisions to cut back on their crops, or not plant at all, University of New South Wales food and health professor Johannes le Coutre said the impact of the squeeze on fuel and fertiliser would be felt for months.

"If less is being planted, we have ripple effects," Dr le Coutre said.

"Late 2026, early 2027… we will be seeing, most likely, higher prices for flour-based goods, bread, beer and malt.

"Livestock will be indirectly affected later on with an increase in meat, eggs and dairy through higher feed costs."

Keeping farmers farming

CSIRO Agriculture and Food Research Unit deputy director Alison Bentley said Australia's agricultural production remained strong, but it was not yet clear what impact the crisis would have.

Alison Bentley says the CSIRO is working with farmers on different fertiliser options. (Supplied: CSIRO)

"There's a lot of people working on the modelling of what these decisions that growers are making now will have on the supply of important commodity crops," Dr Bentley said.

In the meantime, CSIRO scientists are helping farmers innovate, including trialling biologically sourced fertilisers, such as seaweed.

"There's quite a lot of research still to be done to understand it, but the growers are looking at what products are already in the market that can help them," Dr Bentley said.

World.title: Australia urged to start providing cooked lunches in schools
World.content:
The frantic morning tradition of packing children's lunch boxes could become a thing of the past if an ambitious push for a universal school lunch program is successful.

Australia is one of the few high-income countries in the world where students are not provided with a free meal each day at school.

At a time of rising cost-of-living pressures, one not-for-profit program in Tasmania has been serving about 21,500 healthy, cooked lunchtime meals to students each week.

Founded by Julie Dunbabin in 2020, the School Food Matters lunch program caters for 60 public schools across the state, with the free meals largely funded by the Tasmanian government.

School lunch program manager Julie Dunbabbin. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Dunbabin would like to see the scheme expanded with a nationwide rollout.

"That's the dream and that's what we'll be calling for action on at the end of the day," she said.

" What Tasmania has done is develop a very strong role model [for other states] to copy. "

Ms Dunbabin said the program had delivered anecdotal improvements in student behaviour, attendance rates and social connections, with firmer research being conducted.

These are the types of lunches students can expect. (Supplied: School Food Matters)

The meals provided by the School Food Matters program cost about $10 to prepare, which includes ingredients, delivery, staffing and equipment.

While the meals delivered through the scheme are free, Ms Dunbabin warned a wider rollout would likely require parents to contribute a small fee to each meal.

"For sustainability, parent co-payment is going to be really crucial," she said.

"It's not the government's job to pay for everything, so I think that having that buy-in from families would be such a positive thing and it happens everywhere else."

Ms Dunbabin said a fee of about $5 from parents for each meal could be enough to help support a national rollout.

"If you look at what it costs to kit out a lunch box, it's usually around $7 to $11, so a school lunch meal is more affordable in the long run," she said.

A sample of some of the school lunch menus. (Supplied: School Food Matters)

How important is the lunchtime meal?

Food insecurity is a growing problem within Australia, making it increasingly difficult for a growing number of families to provide regular, healthy meals.

Katherine Kent, a senior lecturer in nutrition and dietetics at the University of Wollongong, said this trend was evident within the nation's schools.

"We know that parents are really struggling to put food into the lunch box that is healthy and nutritious," Dr Kent said.

" Kids often come to school with not very much healthy food, maybe lots of packets of food, chips and biscuits, and things that are not giving kids the nutrition they need. "

Dr Katherine Kent says "kids often come to school with … packets of food, chips and biscuits". (Supplied)

That nutritional lack could then have ramifications on the rest of the student's day, impacting their learning.

Macquarie University's Miriam Williams, who is a member of the global Community Economies Institute, said missing out on a nutritious lunchtime meal could have a "huge impact" on concentration, health and general wellbeing.

"One third of all meals are consumed at school for children, and the food that we eat … is integral for our ability function well in the classroom," Dr Williams said.

Some of the countries that provide universal school lunch programs include Japan, Sweden and Estonia, as well as parts of the United States and the United Kingdom.

Dr Miriam Williams says a third of all meals consumed by school-aged children are eaten at school.

Means testing to ensure equitable access

Introducing a universal school lunch program across Australia would deliver significant improvements for students, according to Dr Kent.

"There's a real opportunity for a school lunch program to ensure students have at least one nutritious meal per day," she said.

"Often it's going to be a meal that is full of protein, vegetables and healthy carbohydrates."

Dr Kent said her studies indicated about 90 per cent of parents in New South Wales were supportive of a lunch program and willing to pay about $5 per meal.

However, she said it was important to ensure any model had universal access for all students.

"We wouldn't want children whose families are unable to pay $5 a day for their child to miss out on that nutritional meal," Dr Kent said.

" Because they are the families that probably need the most help getting a nutritional meal for their child. "

Dr Williams said if Australia were to adopt the lunch program, it would be an "excellent structural solution" to the cost-of-living pressures on families, and would help ensure children have "the best start possible".

She said different models should be considered, including one where parents can choose from a range of payment options.

"It could be means-tested, some families pay $5 or $10, while other families have it free and subsidised in order to roll it out," Dr Williams said.

Dr Williams said the scheme could also create employment opportunities, address sustainability and food waste issues, as well as give time-poor parents extra time in the morning.

'Falling through the policy gaps'

A national school food summit was held in Hobart on Monday, in which Ms Dunbabin was the keynote speaker.

This is what free school lunches look like, as Tasmania expands program Students are trying new foods as more schools are getting free lunches, and teachers say it's benefiting not just their bellies.

Speaking to about 150 delegates from across the country, including health researchers, canteen managers and teachers, she called for the creation of a universal program.

"The federal government would get great value in being involved in supporting this program," Ms Dunbabin said.

Dr Kent said Tasmania was "leading the way" with its school lunch program and she would advocate for a similar investment on the mainland.

"Food insecurity and school meals is in everybody's interest but it's not yet anybody's responsibility and that means it's falling through the policy gaps," she said.

"We need to bring more of our state government politicians and departments together to work on a coordinated approach to see what's possible."

Loading...

School Food Matters executive officer Kirsty Grierson said the non-profit organisation was currently focused on expanding within Tasmania.

She said co-contributions from parents had been considered during the business case, but there were no plans to introduce it at this stage.

"We're very much focused on what is happening in Tasmania and really refining the program," Ms Grierson said.

Over the past two years, the Tasmanian government has invested about $14.6 million to help deliver the free school lunch program.

World.title: Three dead in boating accident off NSW coast as search for survivors continues
World.content:
Three people have died after a boating accident at Ballina on the northern NSW coast, with a search continuing for survivors.

Emergency services were contacted about 6:15pm on Monday, after a member of the public reported a yacht having difficulties off the South Ballina breakwall.

Marine Rescue NSW responded, but its vessel rolled while crossing the Ballina Bar in rough conditions.

In a statement, NSW Police said three people had died.

One man had to be winched to safety by a rescue helicopter and was treated for chest injuries.

Three other people made it to shore without assistance and were taken to the Lismore Base Hospital for observation.

It is unknown how many people were on the yacht, which police now believe has sunk.

Tweed Heads Water Police and general duties officers from Richmond Police District are on scene.

Marine Area Command is conducting a search-and-rescue effort from its Balmain headquarters.

Additional assistance will be provided by the AMSA Challenger jet and the Rescue Helicopter from Lismore.

World.title: Four Australians stuck on cruise ship after suspected deadly hantavirus outbreak
World.content:
WorldAfricaHealth Four Australians stuck on cruise ship after suspected deadly hantavirus outbreak Olivia Le Poidevin Daniel Lo Surdo and May 5, 2026 — 6:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four Australians are stranded on a luxury cruise ship being held off West Africa after three passengers died in a suspected outbreak of the deadly hantavirus. The cruise operator confirmed the Australians were among 149 people on board, from 23 countries. The Dutch-flagged MV Hondius remains moored off the coast of Cape Verde in West Africa as local health authorities assess the situation. The MV Hondius cruise ship is anchored at a port in Praia, Cape Verde, on Monday. AP Medics were working on Monday (Cape Verde time) to evacuate two people with symptoms of hantavirus. A Dutch couple and a German national have died, while others fell ill, including a Briton who left the vessel and was being treated in South Africa, authorities added. The Netherlands’ National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM), which is assisting with the outbreak, said hantavirus had been confirmed in one of the patients showing symptoms.



A source briefed on the matter said that the Dutch woman who died had tested positive for the virus as well. RIVM said it was still unclear if the other people with symptoms also had the virus, or if the other deaths were also caused by the virus. Loading Hantavirus, which can cause fatal respiratory illness, can be spread when particles from rodent droppings or urine become airborne. It does not transfer easily between humans. There are ​no specific drugs to treat the disease, so treatment focuses on supportive care, ​including putting ⁠patients on ventilators in severe cases.



The World Health Organization said the risk to the wider public was low and there was no need for panic or travel restrictions. But authorities in the island nation of Cape Verde said they had not allowed the MV Hondius to dock as a precaution. “We’re not just headlines: we’re people with families, with lives, with people waiting for us at home,” Jake Rosmarin, a US travel blogger, said in a tearful Instagram video post from the ship on Monday. “There is a lot of uncertainty and that is the hardest part,” he said. A spokesperson for the ship’s Netherlands-based operator, Oceanwide Expeditions, said that, as a precaution, all passengers were instructed to remain inside their cabins to prevent any potential spread of the virus. Although human-to-human transmission is rare, the incubation period can last several weeks, meaning some people may not yet be showing symptoms.



Oceanwide Expeditions was trying to arrange the repatriation of two crew members with symptoms of the disease – one British and one Dutch – along with the body of the German national and a “guest closely associated with the deceased” who does not have symptoms. The company said it was looking into whether passengers could be screened and disembarked on the islands of Las Palmas and Tenerife. Spanish authorities said they had not yet received a request for the ship to dock and disembark passengers there. The Dutch Foreign Affairs Ministry, which Oceanwide Expeditions said would be the one making the request, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Hondius left Ushuaia in southern Argentina in March, according to company documentation, on a voyage marketed as an Antarctic nature expedition, with berth prices ranging from 14,000 to 22,000 euros ($23,000-$36,000). It travelled past mainland Antarctica, the Falklands, South Georgia, Nightingale Island, Tristan, St Helena, and Ascension before reaching Cape Verdean waters on May 3.



South Africa’s Health Department confirmed two of the dead were Dutch nationals: a 70-year-old man, who died on St Helena on April 11, and his wife, 69, who died in South Africa after collapsing at O.R. Tambo International Airport. Related Article Holidays Three people have died from a virus on a cruise ship. Are ships as high-risk as we might think? The British man being treated in a private clinic in Johannesburg became ill on April 27, while the German victim on the ship died on May 2, Oceanwide Expeditions said. Hantavirus usually begins with flu-like symptoms, such as fatigue and fever, one to eight weeks after exposure. A spokesperson for the RIVM said the source of the outbreak was unclear. “You could imagine, for example, that rats on board the ship transmitted the virus,” he said.



“But another possibility is that during a stop somewhere in South America, people were infected, for instance via mice, and became ill that way.” Daniel Bausch, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute in Switzerland, said there was some evidence of human-to-human transmission in the Andes Virus, a species of hantavirus found in Argentina and Chile. The MV Hondius. AP “So it’s significant that this cruise ship started its journey in Argentina,” he said. “The good news is ... this is not going to be a big outbreak,” he said.

World.title: Victoria to rewrite Sentencing Act as next year’s surplus takes a hit
World.content:
Victoria is forecasting a slashed surplus, rising debt and steeper interest bills, as Labor commits to an election year overhaul of the state’s sentencing laws. Tuesday’s state budget, which will also extend stamp duty discounts, will forecast a surplus for the next financial year of $1 billion – $900 million less than predicted in December. State Treasurer Jaclyn Symes in her office on Monday with the 2026-2027 budget papers. Joe Armao Figures provided to The Age by the government forecast Victoria will record its first surplus since the pandemic, at more than $700 million for 2025-26. The figure is predicted to grow to $1 billion in 2026-27. The state did not provide figures for the remaining budget years but said surpluses would average $1.7 billion over the forward estimates out to 2030.



Victoria’s net debt was forecast to reach $192 billion by 2028-29 in the latest update released in December. A higher figure is expected in 2029-30. “Labor’s budget is in surplus while continuing to invest in the frontline services Victorians rely on,” Treasurer Jaclyn Symes told The Age. The $900 million revision to the 2026-27 surplus comes after a flurry of spending announcements over the past month, including $432 million to extend free public transport until the end of May and introduce half-price fares for the rest of 2026. Premier Jacinta Allan said the state could afford cost-of-living relief because it was still delivering operating surpluses and the economy was growing. Operating results do not include capital expenditure, such as roads and hospitals.



Related Article Victorian budget Boxed in: The harsh budget reality facing Victoria and the two costs we can’t rein in Victoria is expected to spend over $10 billion more than the revenue it generates this year, once infrastructure projects that can be financed by debt are allowed for. The pre-election budget will also allocate $3 million for an independent review of the Sentencing Act that underpins the penalties handed down by courts, a sign that crime is still on voters’ minds despite the government’s “adult time for violent crime” policies aimed at cracking down on young offenders. Although sentencing laws have been reviewed before, the government says this is the first comprehensive review of the entire act since it was first legislated in 1991. The Sentencing Advisory Council will conduct the review and be tasked with ensuring the laws are clear, more consistent and in line with community expectations.



Advice will include whether the act meets 21st-century expectations and how sentencing can better interact with victims of crime. The council will also be asked to spend time on specific issues causing concern, including penalties for those who harm people trying to provide assistance, known as Good Samaritan laws. Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny. An independent review of the Sentencing Act is to be allocated $3 million. Eamon Gallagher “Sentencing absolutely needs to reflect community expectations – but the act hasn’t been reviewed with that aim in mind since 1991,” Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny said. “It’s no wonder many Victorians think sentencing doesn’t reflect our modern challenges. We’ll rewrite the act following the advice from experts, police and the public, because under Labor, community safety comes first,” she said.



Once the review is completed, the government will rewrite the act. The process is focused on longer-term changes and will not prevent the state from making urgent changes to justice laws when needed. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election In Nepean, one in four voters chose One Nation. Both major parties should be worried Separate to this work, the Victorian Law Reform Commission will be asked to provide advice on the state’s laws protecting emergency workers, following another attack on a paramedic last week. Tuesday’s budget will also extend a discount on stamp duty for Victorians buying off-the-plan apartments, units and townhouses for another six months, at a cost of $32.7 million. The discount was due to expire in October, two years after it was announced, but it will now apply for contracts signed before April 21, 2027.



Under the scheme, buyers can deduct the cost of construction from the total value of their property, which is used to determine stamp duty. Related Article Federal budget Labor insiders coy on income tax cuts, as government casts broken promise as virtuous A $620,000 purchase of an apartment expected to cost $465,000 to build would be assessed at $155,000. This would reduce stamp duty to $4000 and create a saving of $28,000. Savings will depend on how much construction takes place on or after the contract date. A property that is half-complete will incur stamp duty on the value already finished, but a buyer can receive the concession for the other half. An apartment that hasn’t started will be able to access the full cut. Kilkenny, who is also planning minister, said the extension would maintain momentum for the creation of new homes.



“Labor is delivering a tax cut for home buyers. Do the Liberals support it, or will they cut it?” she said. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said on Monday that the operating surplus did not consider the true spending in the budget. “It’s all well and good for the premier and the treasurer to stand up and talk about a $700 million operating surplus, but it does nothing to manage the debt bomb that is running under this government,” she said. World.title: Middle East tensions ignite, oil surges on first day of Trump’s new ‘project’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Middle East tensions ignite, oil surges on first day of Trump’s new ‘project’ Michael Koziol May 5, 2026 — 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Iran has fired missiles at civilian targets in the United Arab Emirates and appeared to strike ships in the Strait of Hormuz as tensions reignited in the Middle East and the price of oil shot up another 5 per cent. Iran’s renewed aggression came on the first day of US President Donald Trump’s so-called “Project Freedom” to encourage vessels to risk transiting the log-jammed strait by offering a form of military protection, with Trump now calling on Indo-Pacific allies for help. A container ship sits at anchor as a small motorboat passes in the foreground in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday. AP The US responded in kind, sinking seven Iranian “small boats”, Trump said, and threatening further strikes. It represents the greatest challenge so far to a four-week-old ceasefire between the US, Israel and Iran that has constrained fighting but failed to lead to a peace agreement or sustained negotiations between the parties.



The UAE’s Ministry of Defence said its air defence systems intercepted 12 ballistic missiles and three cruise missiles launched from Iran on Monday (US time), as well as four drones. The country’s Foreign Ministry condemned the “dangerous escalation” from Iran and reserved its rights to respond. Three Indian nationals were injured in the drone and missile attacks, it added. Loading An “advanced fire” broke out in the petroleum industrial area of Fujairah following an Iranian drone attack, the Fujairah Media Office said. Bloomberg reported the facility struck was a VTTI oil terminal partly owned by IFM Investors, the Australian investment house. Meanwhile, there was an explosion and fire on board a cargo vessel operated by South Korean liner HMM in the Strait of Hormuz, the South Korean Foreign Ministry said.



Trump appeared to confirm the incident was related to an Iranian attack as he called on Seoul to assist in the military mission to guide ships through the waterway. “Iran has taken some shots at unrelated Nations with respect to the Ship Movement, PROJECT FREEDOM, including a South Korean Cargo Ship,” he posted on social media. US President Donald Trump and his son, Donald Trump Jr, returning to the White House on Sunday. Bloomberg “Perhaps it’s time for South Korea to come and join the mission! We’ve shot down seven small Boats or, as they like to call them, ‘fast’ Boats. It’s all they have left. Other than the South Korean Ship, there has been, at this moment, no damage going through the Strait.” Trump announced the initiative on the weekend, saying the US Navy would guide ships safely out of the strait. Many have lingered in the Persian Gulf for two months since the war’s outbreak and are running low on food.



The US president said the exercise was a humanitarian gesture and anyone who interfered would “have to be dealt with forcefully”. He later told Fox News that if Iran attacked American vessels involved in the exercise, “they’ll be blown off the face of the earth”. As part of Project Freedom, American guided-missile destroyers have moved through the strait into the Persian Gulf, although they are not believed to be providing a physical escort for ships wishing to exit the Gulf. US Central Command – the military division in the Middle East – said it had “reached out” to dozens of ships and shipping companies to encourage them to move through the strait.



Two US-flagged merchant ships successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz as a first step, Centcom said. Iran denied any such crossings had taken place. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: Jefferson Lewis due in court charged with murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby; UAE says Iran has resumed drone and missile attacks “The distinction, from my perspective, is crystal clear,” said Centcom commander Brad Cooper. “US forces are helping the international community in restoring the flow of global commerce, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, on the other hand, is doing everything it can to terrorise and threaten global shipping”. The promise of US Navy assistance failed to calm markets amid the renewed hostilities on Monday (US time), with the price of Brent crude climbing nearly 6 per cent to just below $US115 a barrel. In the US, the national average price of petrol rose above $US4.45 a gallon ($1.64 a litre). Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said that when faced with a choice between escalating or capitulating, Tehran would choose to escalate.

World.title: ‘The most powerful presence is absence’: Dorothy Porter reimagined
World.content:
CultureMusicArts ‘The most powerful presence is absence’: Dorothy Porter reimagined Will Cox May 5, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sophia Brous and Andrea Goldsmith are talking about muses. “Oh my God,” says Goldsmith. “It’s a shocking term. But did I inspire her best work? Of course!” She laughs. Goldsmith’s partner was Dorothy Porter, the revered Australian poet who passed away in 2008. Porter’s final published work, The Bee Hut (2009), is the basis for Life Lines, a new song cycle by Brous, performed with Paul Grabowsky, to premiere at the Melbourne Writers Festival. Sophia Brous (left) and Andrea Goldsmith. Ruby Alexander Nearly two decades after her death, Porter is very much the centre of the conversation. As she writes in “Egypt”, the opening poem of The Bee Hut, “The most powerful presence is absence.” Life Lines is part of Brous’ Set Pieces series of song cycles inspired by poets. The libretto is written in advance from existing works, but the music emerges through improvisation.



Past performances have been built from the words of Argentinian Russian-Jewish poet Alejandra Pizarnik and Polish poet Debora Vogel. It was Veronica Sullivan, director of the Melbourne Writers Festival, who suggested she turn her eye to Dorothy Porter. Notes and deliberations about the show, inspired by the work of the late Dorothy Porter, one of Australia’s most revered poets. Ruby Alexander “She’s such a revered figure in the psyche of the country, and in my own psyche,” says Brous. “I said, ‘Sure, but ... am I allowed? Is that OK?’” It was. She met with Goldsmith, guardian of Porter’s work, who gave her approval to the piece, and lent the title, Life Lines. After Brous and Goldsmith met and settled on the poems that would form the piece, Brous recalls getting an email from Goldsmith. “It said, ‘You should, you do with this work what you wish,’” which is incredible,” says Brous.



“Which Dot would have said too,” says Goldsmith. “She was always a very generous collaborator. She loved what another artist could bring to her words.” One of Australia’s most influential poets, Porter is best known for her 1994 verse novel, The Monkey’s Mask, which has been adapted for stage, radio and film. Music was always an influence on her work, and vice versa. This latest project, Goldsmith says, is exactly the sort of thing Porter would have loved. Related Article Literature How Shaun Tan’s book with no storyline inspired so many tattoos “From the very beginning, composers have recognised how musical Dot’s poetry is,” says Goldsmith. “There’s something about her words, and as you read them you can actually feel the musicality.” Porter collaborated with Grabowsky for the 2005 album Before Time Could Change Us, with vocals by Katie Noonan. Since Porter’s death, Goldsmith has overseen several musical collaborations based on the poet’s work. A collaboration with Tim Finn which Porter began in the 1990s finally premiered in 2016 as The Fiery Maze. Further musical adaptations of her work have been performed by Jonathan Mills and Brett Dean.



Brous has known Grabowsky for years, and sought him out to collaborate on this project even before she had settled on Porter as the piece’s inspiration. That he’d worked with Porter came as a surprise. “I believe in creative, in the serendipity of things,” says Brous. Porter often wrote to music, too. Goldsmith shows us a playlist that Porter made for her of the songs she had in mind while writing The Bee Hut. It’s the first time Brous has seen it. It’s an eclectic list, full of big feelings, from AC/DC to Antony and the Johnsons. “I would ask Dot about the music that she used, because I could so rarely see a connection with the writing,” says Goldsmith. “It operated at a very visceral level for her. It took her out of herself.” Brous is a musician who lives between Melbourne and New York, where she is part of the improvisational band Exo-Tech, formed with Kiwi musician Kimbra.



“This project, for me, is a way of playfully subverting audience’s expectations,” says Brous. “I’d be very happy if no one in the audience knows that the piece is being created in the moment. It doesn’t matter.” Poet Dorothy Porter. Cathryn Tremain The collection that Brous was most drawn to, The Bee Hut, is an intimate book which grapples with mortality and loss. “But it has a certain giddy romance throughout as well,” says Brous. No two performances of Life Lines will be alike, but Brous is uneasy about the word “improv”, which carries jazz connotations, or “jam”, which sounds too loose. “We’re letting the words be the scenery, the environments around the text,” says Brous. The term “emergent composition” sits well, as does Brous’ comparison to American artist Alexander Calder’s hanging mobiles. It implies balance, movement. “It’s a dance,” says Brous. “We’re in a dialogue that is emergent, and that takes a great deal of trust and relinquishing of control as well.”



Goldsmith is excited about the possibilities. “What is actually going to happen on the night is going to be a real surprise to me,” she says. “I mean, of course I know Paul’s music, and now I know Sophia’s, but it’s emerging in the moment. It’s quite extraordinary.” She once saw Grabowsky perform an improvisation based on the Goldberg Variations. “He started in a known place, and he ended in a known place, and he took on a journey that Bach would have been proud of,” she says. “It was unbelievable.” Goldsmith believes in seeing Porter’s work take on new forms. She once wrote that Porter wanted to see poetry “displayed in neon”. “She was a typical poet, in that she saw poetry as the pinnacle of writing,” says Goldsmith. “Her aim was to bring poetry from the back of the shop, where it was mouldering with the craft books, up to the window.” “In this series so far, I’ve worked with writing that I had no personal connection to, but this has been a much more personal process,” Brous says. “And to have Dot’s partner – in life and in creativity - able to talk me through every single poem … I’ve never experienced this kind of intimacy as a background.” Life Lines is at the State Library of Victoria on Friday, as part of Melbourne Writers Festival.

World.title: ASX set to fall, oil jumps on war uncertainty; RBA decision ahead; GameStop makes $78b bid for eBay
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall, oil jumps on war uncertainty; RBA decision ahead; GameStop makes $78b bid for eBay Stan Choe May 5, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is falling from its record heights while oil prices jump following escalations in the Middle East that may be undermining the ceasefire in the war with Iran. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent, coming off its latest all-time high. The Dow Jones was down 528 points, or 1.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.2 per cent lower. Wall Street has fallen to start the week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 4.53am AEST pointing to a fall of 75 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Monday. The Reserve Bank announces its interest rates decision on Tuesday afternoon, with higher inflation expected to force the central bank to inflict a third consecutive hike. Financial markets put the chance of a rate rise at 75 per cent with at least one more increase expected by October. The overnight action was strong in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude leaped 5.6 per cent to $US114.21. It jolted higher after the United Arab Emirates said it came under attack by Iran for the first time since the fragile ceasefire took hold in early April. The attacks appeared to be in response to US President Donald Trump’s latest efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.



Iran’s closure of the strait has kept oil tankers pent up in the Persian Gulf and away from customers worldwide. That in turn has sent the price of Brent soaring from roughly $US70 per barrel before the war. Trump said Sunday that the United States would guide ships through the strait, which could get oil flowing again and bring down its price. But prices instead climbed after Iranian news agencies claimed Monday that Iran had struck a US Navy vessel southeast of the Strait of Hormuz, accusing it of “violating maritime security and navigation norms.” The US military rejected the claim and then said that two American-flagged merchant ships had successfully transited through the Strait of Hormuz. Even with all the uncertainty about how long the war with Iran will last, the US stock market has managed to power to record after record. Hope is still high on Wall Street that the global economy can avoid a worst-case scenario because of the war. And in the meantime, companies continue to deliver big growth in profits. That’s key because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. The strength so far this reporting season has been broad-based and not confined to just the Big Tech superstars that dominate the market. The median stock in the S&P 500 is tracking for the best growth since 2021, according to Savita Subramanian, a strategist at Bank of America.



Tyson Foods joined the list Monday of those topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue during the latest quarter. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America The cracks are widening in Trump’s America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist It sold less beef than it did a year ago, but it did so at prices that were 11.5 per cent higher, so its total beef revenue edged up. It also sold more chicken and pork than a year earlier, at slightly higher prices. Its stock rose 3.9 per cent. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings likewise delivered a better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But it’s feeling the effects of the war, which has not only raised pressure on fuel prices but also pushed some customers to think twice about travel plans, particularly to Europe. The cruise operator said some “execution missteps” also have bookings below where it would like, and its stock fell 9.2 per cent.



GameStop slumped after it said it wants to buy eBay for about $US56 billion ($78 billion) in cash and stock, an offer that . Coming into the day, eBay had a total market value that was nearly quadruple GameStop’s. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing Seven’s Game of Thrones claims another victim Colin Kruger Senior business reporter GameStop said it has already built a 5 per cent stake in eBay and sees opportunities to cut $US2 billion in annual costs quickly. GameStop, whose stock briefly soared to market-shaking heights during the meme stock craze of 2021, fell 7.8 per cent, while eBay rose 5.7 per cent. Several Big Tech stocks were strong, continuing a big run for companies involved in artificial-intelligence technology. Micron Technology gained 5.8 per cent for one of the biggest gains in the S&P 500. Oracle rallied 5.7 per cent, and Sandisk climbed 4.4 per cent. In stock markets abroad, gains for tech stocks helped indexes jump 5.1 per cent in South Korea and 1.2 per cent in Hong Kong, while markets were closed in mainland China and Japan for holidays.



European indexes fared worse, and France’s CAC 40 fell 1.7 per cent. In the bond market, Treasury yield jumped up as oil prices climbed. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.45 per cent from 4.39 per cent late on Friday. It was at just 3.97 per cent before the war began, and the rise has made mortgages and other kinds of loans for US households and businesses more expensive.
